Artificial Intelligence and Infrared Sensors Detect Plant Allergens in Food Prototype

Researchers from the eVIDA research group at the University of Deusto have completed a functional prototype capable of detecting lipid transfer proteins in food by combining near-infrared spectroscopy with signal-processing algorithms and artificial intelligence. Developed under the smartJAN project in collaboration with technology firm Kernet and Fundación Miranda, the system targets a family of plant proteins containing allergens that can trigger severe allergic reactions, which are notably prevalent across the Mediterranean region.

The technical investigation focused on evaluating the feasibility of detecting allergenic proteins belonging to the lipid transfer protein family found across many plant-derived foods. The research team specifically analyzed Pru p 3, an allergenic protein found primarily in peach skin, along with Ara h 9, an allergen present in peanuts, as the primary model targets for testing the screening approach.

To perform the non-destructive analysis, the system shines light directly onto the food sample and records how that light is reflected back. This optical interaction produces a distinctive spectral fingerprint that the integrated artificial intelligence system interprets immediately to identify whether potentially harmful substances are present, removing the requirement to destroy the food item or transport samples to an external laboratory for testing.

According to research lead Begoña García-Zapirain, the underlying detection methodology holds potential for applications beyond the specific plant allergens evaluated during the initial project. Prior experimental tests demonstrated that the sensor configuration could detect gluten as well as bacterial contamination in meat, suggesting the platform may eventually support the early identification of common foodborne pathogens such as Salmonella.

With financial backing from the Basque Government’s Hazitek programme, the initial development phase and prototype validation have concluded, positioning the technology for potential industrial translation. The development team designed the device specifically for integration into industrial quality control lines, distribution networks, and institutional catering operations rather than for direct domestic or consumer use.

The multi-sector consortium included Fundación Miranda to address a social dimension centered on healthcare and nutrition for adults aged 65 and older, a demographic group where mitigating food-related risks and adhering to precise dietary requirements are particularly vital. Next steps toward commercialization will depend on industrial interest in converting the validated laboratory prototype into a standardized commercial testing device once reliability validation protocols are established.

The published findings from the initiative, detailing the artificial intelligence framework for non-specific lipid transfer protein detection using near-infrared spectral data, appeared in the journal Food Analytical Methods following peer-reviewed technical evaluation. By complementing conventional laboratory assays, the rapid screening method is intended to accelerate quality verification workflows and reinforce safety oversight within commercial food supply chains.

Subject of Research: Near-infrared spectroscopy and artificial intelligence for detecting allergenic plant proteins in food

Article Title: Deusto explores the use of artificial intelligence and smart sensors to improve food safety quickly and affordably
